subsection: 2. Burning fossil fuels and using alternative energy sources

notes.b: Fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas formed from ancient living things) supply about four-fifths of the world's primary energy (the energy taken straight from nature before conversion) in the 2020s. Their production is concentrated in a few places, so most countries must import them.
points: The Middle East (e.g. Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq) holds about half the world's proven oil reserves (oil known to be recoverable). Venezuela has the largest proven reserves of any single country.
The USA has been the world's largest oil producer since the late 2010s, through shale oil and gas (trapped in rock and released by fracking, which fractures the rock with pressurised liquid).
Russia is one of the largest gas exporters. Qatar is a leading exporter of liquefied natural gas (LNG, gas cooled to a liquid so that ships can carry it).
China produces and consumes about half the world's coal.
Fossil fuels are traded over long distances by tanker, pipeline and LNG ship, so importers depend on exporters for their energy security (a steady, affordable supply of energy).
notes.tip: Be ready to name two fossil fuels and to explain what a fossil fuel is. Learn the producers above, with the Middle East's share of oil and China's share of coal, for data questions.

notes.b: Energy use is very uneven across the world. It follows wealth and industry, and the pattern is shifting towards Asia.
points: Developed countries use far more energy per person than developing countries. Demand is now growing fastest in Asia, notably China and India, because their economies and populations are growing.
The USA, Canada and Australia use many times more energy per person than India or most of sub-Saharan Africa.
China has been the world's largest CO2 (carbon dioxide) emitter in total since the mid-2000s, but the USA emits far more CO2 per person.
notes.tip: Exams use energy-mix and emissions charts. Keep total emissions (China is largest) separate from emissions per person (the USA is far higher).

notes.h: Pollutants released by burning fossil fuels
notes.b: Burning a fossil fuel releases the carbon and impurities locked inside it. Each pollutant causes a different problem, so keep them apart.
points: Carbon dioxide (CO2) is the main greenhouse gas released, and it drives global warming.
Sulphur dioxide (SO2), mainly from coal and heavy oil (thick, impure oil), is a cause of acid rain.
Nitrogen oxides (NOx), mainly from vehicles and power stations, are also a cause of acid rain.
Smoke, fine particles (soot, tiny solid specks that can be breathed deep into the lungs) and carbon monoxide are released as well.
notes.tip: Acid rain is caused by SO2 and NOx, not by CO2. CO2 causes global warming, and the ozone hole is caused by CFCs. Keep all three separate.

notes.b: The greenhouse effect is the natural trapping of heat by gases in the atmosphere. Burning fossil fuels adds extra gas to it.
points: CO2 traps heat in the atmosphere, so extra CO2 from burning fossil fuels enhances the greenhouse effect and causes global warming. There is more on this in Environmental pollution.
notes.tip: If asked for a negative effect of CO2, say global warming. For a question on the impact of burning fossil fuels, give global warming briefly and spend your time on acid rain and smog.

notes.h: Acid rain: formation and spread in Europe
notes.b: Acid rain is a transboundary problem (one that crosses national borders): the countries that cause it are often not the ones that suffer.
points: Normal rain is slightly acidic, at about pH 5.6, because CO2 dissolves in it naturally. Acid rain is rain with a pH below 5.6, not below pH 7.
SO2 and NOx dissolve in water vapour to form sulphuric and nitric acids. These fall as wet deposition in rain, or as dry deposition of acidic particles and gases.
Sources include coal-fired power stations, heavy industry and vehicles, because all of them burn fuels that contain sulphur or release nitrogen oxides.

Emissions from Britain and Germany were carried by the prevailing south-westerly winds (the usual wind direction) to Norway and Sweden, which is why Scandinavia suffered from other countries' pollution.

The Black Triangle, the border region of former East Germany, Poland and Czechia, had lignite-burning power stations (lignite is a low-grade, smoky coal) that caused severe forest death in the 1970s and 1980s.
notes.tip: Acid rain is any rain below about pH 5.6, not below pH 7, because all natural rain is slightly acidic. Show that the country that suffers is often not the one that pollutes, using Scandinavia.

notes.b: Acid rain harms living things, buildings and people. The damage can appear far from the source, because the wind carries the pollution across borders.
points: Forest damage: needle and leaf loss, and nutrients leached (washed out) from the soil. German forests, such as the Black Forest, were reported dying in the 1980s (Waldsterben, meaning forest death).
Lake acidification: thousands of Scandinavian lakes were acidified and lost their fish. Aluminium released from the soil by the acid kills fish.
Limestone and marble buildings and statues dissolve, through the same process as the chemical weathering of limestone (carbonation, where weak acid reacts with the rock).
Corrosion of metal, for example, and respiratory (breathing) problems in people.
notes.tip: For European detail, name Scandinavian lakes, German forests including the Black Forest, and the Black Triangle.

notes.b: Because acid rain crosses borders, responses had to be international as well as national. They work either by cutting emissions or by repairing the damage.
points: The 1979 Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution, signed at UNECE (the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe) in Geneva, was an international agreement on air pollution that crosses borders.
EU directives (laws binding on member states) limit emissions from large power stations.

Flue-gas desulphurisation (scrubbers, which remove SO2 from the smoke before it leaves the chimney) is used at power stations. Moneypoint, Co. Clare, opened in 1985 and had scrubbers fitted in the late 2000s.
Low-sulphur fuels cut SO2 at source. Catalytic converters (exhaust devices that reduce NOx) became compulsory on new petrol cars in the EU in 1993.
Sweden and Norway have limed acidified lakes (added lime to neutralise the acid) since the 1970s and 1980s.
Countries switched from coal to gas and renewables, which release little or no SO2.
Outcome: European SO2 emissions have fallen by well over three-quarters since 1990, and many lakes are recovering.
notes.tip: Higher Level answers on fossil-fuel impact are expected to include responses as well as causes and effects. Give the 1979 Convention, scrubbers at Moneypoint, catalytic converters and the fall in SO2 since 1990.

notes.b: Smog is smoke mixed with fog. It builds up when smoke from home fires cannot escape upwards.
points: Burning coal and turf in homes releases smoke and fine particles, because the fuel burns incompletely in an open fire.
In calm, cold winter weather an anticyclone (a high-pressure system with settled air) creates a temperature inversion, where a layer of warm air sits above cold air near the ground.
The inversion traps the smoke near the ground, because the warm layer stops it rising and blowing away. This forms smog.
Smog causes bronchitis, asthma, heart and lung disease, and extra deaths, because the smoke and fine particles are breathed in.

notes.b: Smog led governments to ban smoky fuels in city areas. London's disaster in 1952 was the earlier precedent, and Dublin's ban is the Irish case study.
points: London's Great Smog, in December 1952, caused about 4,000 deaths at the time. Later estimates are far higher.
The Great Smog led to the UK Clean Air Act 1956, which created smokeless zones (areas where smoky fuel may not be burned).
Dublin suffered severe winter smogs in the early 1980s from household coal burning, which led to the ban.
The sale of smoky (bituminous) coal was banned in Dublin from 1 September 1990. Black smoke levels fell by about 70%.
The ban covered smoky coal only, so smokeless fuel and turf could still be burned in Dublin at first.
A study published in The Lancet in 2002 estimated that the ban was linked to about 350 fewer deaths a year in Dublin from respiratory and heart disease.
The ban was extended to Cork in 1995, and in stages to other cities and large towns as low-smoke zones. National rules from 2022 further restrict the sale of smoky solid fuels and wet wood.
notes.tip: The Dublin ban was on smoky (bituminous) coal, not on all solid fuel. Keep 'about 350 a year' and 'about 70%' exactly, because the Lancet figure is an estimate. Give 1990 for Dublin and 1995 for Cork, and no dates for other towns.

notes.h: Other impacts of burning fossil fuels
notes.b: Beyond the air pollutants, getting and using fossil fuels harms land, water and rivers.
points: Oil spills during transport, for example from tankers, pollute the sea and coasts. There is more on this in Environmental pollution.
Landscape damage comes from coal mining and peat cutting, which scar and strip the land.
Thermal pollution of rivers is caused by the cooling water of power stations, which is returned to the river warmer than it was taken.

notes.b: Wind turns turbine blades that drive a generator. Turbines are built onshore on land and offshore at sea.
points: Ireland: wind supplied about a third of Irish electricity in the early 2020s, from onshore farms such as Galway Wind Park, Connemara (2017), and from Arklow Bank Wind Park, off Co. Wicklow (2004), Ireland's first offshore wind farm.
Denmark: wind supplies about half of Denmark's electricity.
Advantage: strong, frequent Atlantic winds give Ireland a good wind resource, and wind is the main renewable source in Irish electricity.
Disadvantage: output varies with the wind, and local residents object on grounds of noise, shadow flicker (flickering shadows cast by moving blades) and visual impact.

Disadvantage: Derrybrien, Co. Galway, suffered a peat slide of about 450,000 m³ on 16 October 2003 during construction of a wind farm on bog. The EU Court of Justice fined Ireland in 2019 for the lack of a proper environmental impact assessment (a study of the likely harm before building).
notes.tip: Be ready to explain why wind use has grown, and to give the economic and environmental advantages of wind as one specific source.

notes.b: Hydroelectric power uses falling water to turn turbines, through three main methods.
points: Dams and reservoirs release stored water through turbines at a controlled rate.
Run-of-river schemes use the river's natural flow, so they need little or no stored water.
Pumped storage pumps water uphill at times of low demand and releases it at peak times, so it acts like a store of energy.

Ireland: Ardnacrusha on the River Shannon (Shannon Scheme, opened 1929, built by Siemens) and Turlough Hill, Co. Wicklow (1974), the country's pumped-storage station. Poulaphouca on the Liffey, Inniscarra and Carrigadrohid on the Lee, and Cathaleen's Fall at Ballyshannon on the Erne also generate power.
Advantage: output can be raised quickly at peak times (when demand is highest), as at Turlough Hill.
Disadvantage: Ireland has little hydro potential left for large new schemes.
Norway: hydroelectric power supplies about 90% of its electricity, for example.

Three Gorges Dam, Yangtze River, China: the world's largest power station by installed capacity. It was completed in 2006, fully operational in 2012, and over one million people were relocated. It gives flood control downstream but traps sediment (silt that would otherwise travel downriver).

notes.b: Photovoltaic panels convert sunlight into electricity, and solar thermal panels use sunlight to heat water.
points: Ireland: solar power has grown rapidly since the early 2020s, through large solar farms on farmland and panels on rooftops. SEAI (Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland) grants help homes to install panels.
Disadvantage: Ireland's cloud cover and short winter days limit output, because panels need strong daylight.

notes.b: Waves and tides drive turbines or barrages (dams built across an estuary). The three technologies are different, so do not mix them up.
points: Wave: the Atlantic Marine Energy Test Site off Belmullet, Co. Mayo, is a wave test site.
Tidal barrage: La Rance, Brittany, France, a barrage across the Rance estuary, opened in 1966. It was one of the first and largest tidal power stations.

Tidal stream: SeaGen in Strangford Lough, Co. Down, was installed in 2008 as the world's first commercial-scale tidal-stream turbine, using the fast tidal flow through the narrows. It has since been removed.
Advantage: tides are predictable, because they follow the moon's cycle. Disadvantages: high cost and marine impacts (harm to sea life and habitats).
notes.tip: La Rance is a tidal barrage, SeaGen was a tidal-stream turbine and Belmullet is a wave test site. Do not mix the technologies.

notes.b: Geothermal energy uses heat from the Earth's interior, to heat water or to generate steam.
points: Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge (a plate boundary where the crust is thin) over a hotspot (a rising plume of hot rock). The Hellisheiði power station generates electricity from geothermal water, and about 9 in 10 Icelandic homes are heated by it.
Ireland uses low-temperature heat pumps only, which draw modest heat from the ground.
Advantage: output does not depend on the weather. Disadvantage: high-temperature sources are found only where the crust is hot, as in Iceland.

notes.b: Biomass is organic material (from plants or animal waste) burned or converted to energy.
points: Sources: wood chip, energy crops such as willow and miscanthus, and biogas from slurry and food waste produced by anaerobic digestion (rotting without oxygen).
Biofuels (fuels made from plants) are blended into petrol and diesel, by law in Ireland.
Edenderry, Co. Offaly, was converted from peat to biomass, an example of a power station switching fuel.
Advantage: carbon-neutral in principle, because the crops absorb as much CO2 as they release when burned. Disadvantage: energy crops compete with food production for land.

notes.b: Nuclear power uses fission, the splitting of uranium atoms, to release heat that makes steam to drive turbines. Nuclear is not renewable.
points: France: nuclear power supplies about two-thirds of its electricity.
Advantages: low carbon emissions, so little CO2, plus reliable and large output.
Disadvantages, such as radioactive waste, accident risk, very high cost, and the cost of decommissioning (safely shutting down and dismantling) old reactors.
Chernobyl, Ukraine (then USSR), 26 April 1986: a reactor exploded, and radioactive fallout spread across Europe, including Ireland. A 30 km exclusion zone remains.
Fukushima Daiichi, Japan, 11 March 2011: an earthquake and tsunami knocked out cooling and caused meltdowns.
notes.tip: Nuclear is not renewable. Use Chernobyl and Fukushima as your examples of accident risk.

notes.h: Why Ireland has no nuclear power
notes.b: Ireland has never had a nuclear power station. A combination of law, public opinion and practical limits explains why.
points: The Electricity Regulation Act 1999 bans the use of nuclear fission to generate electricity in Ireland.
The ESB (Electricity Supply Board) planned a nuclear power station at Carnsore Point, Co. Wexford, in the 1970s. It was abandoned after large public protests and was never built.
Other reasons: Ireland's small electricity grid, the high cost, the problem of waste disposal, and fears raised by Chernobyl.
Sellafield, Cumbria, England, a nuclear reprocessing site on the Irish Sea coast, has discharges that Irish governments have long objected to, which adds to Irish unease about nuclear power.
notes.tip: Exams ask why nuclear energy is not used in Ireland. Give the 1999 ban, Carnsore Point and its public protests, the small grid, cost, waste and Chernobyl.

notes.b: Renewable energy comes from sources that are naturally replaced. These advantages apply to wind, hydro, solar, wave, tidal and geothermal power.
points: Renewables are inexhaustible, so supply is secure: the sun, wind, water and tides will not run out.
They produce little or no CO2, SO2 or NOx, so they cause less global warming and acid rain.
They reduce the fossil-fuel import bill and improve energy security.
They create jobs, often in rural areas.
Once a plant is built, the fuel is free.
They help meet EU and national targets and avoid penalties for missing them.
notes.tip: Exams ask for one advantage of renewable energy, and why countries are investing more in renewables. Give each advantage with its reason.

notes.b: Renewables also have costs and limits, and these explain why fossil fuels are still widely used.
points: Renewables are intermittent (not constant), because wind and sun vary, so backup or storage is needed.
The initial cost of building a plant is high.
Turbines and dams have visual impact, and cause noise and local objections.
Remote sites need grid connections (cables linking them to the electricity network).
Some habitats are damaged: birds are killed by turbines, and dams flood valleys. Peat slides can also happen at wind farms on bog.
notes.tip: Exams ask for one disadvantage of renewable energy. Wind-farm conflicts are listed here only as disadvantages.

notes.h: Why renewable energy is crucial for Ireland
notes.b: Ireland imports a large share of its energy, so renewable energy matters for both its environment and its economy.
points: Ireland imported about three-quarters of its energy in the early 2020s, at a cost of billions of euro a year. Renewables reduce this import bill and the exposure to price shocks (sudden rises in world fuel prices).

Ireland must meet its 2030 targets for renewable electricity and emissions. The Climate Action Plan aims for 80% renewable electricity by 2030, and missing EU targets exposes Ireland to the cost of buying compliance.
Energy security improves through interconnectors (cables that link electricity grids): the East-West Interconnector to Wales (2012) and the Celtic Interconnector to France (due in the late 2020s).
Renewables provide jobs and income in rural areas, because wind farms, solar farms and dams are built there.
Green power attracts multinational companies that want renewable electricity.
Cleaner air and water follow from burning less fossil fuel.
notes.tip: This is a Higher Level 30-mark topic, asked as why renewable energy is crucial for Ireland's environment and economy. Cover both environmental and economic points, with the import bill, targets, interconnectors, jobs and multinationals.

notes.b: Map questions ask you to choose and justify a wind-farm site on an Ordnance Survey map, and to explain how conflict may arise. Match each feature of the site to a need of the wind farm.
points: A wind farm needs a high, exposed upland or coastal site with strong winds, because output depends on wind speed.
It should be away from houses, to limit noise and shadow flicker.
It needs an access road close by for construction, and a connection close to the electricity grid, by transmission line (the high-voltage cable that carries power).
It should avoid protected areas and deep peat, because peat can slide when disturbed. It is best placed on land of low farming value.
Conflict arises when a site lies near homes or in a protected or scenic area, so the site must balance wind strength against these constraints.
notes.tip: Choose a site, justify it with these requirements, and explain how conflict may arise from it.

keyTerms.definition: Rain with a pH below 5.6, caused by SO2 and NOx dissolving in water vapour to form acids.
Pollution that crosses national borders, so the country that suffers is often not the one that causes it.
The border region of former East Germany, Poland and Czechia, where lignite-burning power stations caused severe forest death.
A layer of warm air above cold air near the ground, which traps smoke and pollutants and forms smog.
Smoke and fog trapped near the ground by a temperature inversion, harmful to health.
An area where the sale or burning of smoky fuel is restricted to reduce smoke and smog.
A process fitted to power stations that removes sulphur dioxide from the waste gases before they are released.
A hydroelectric method that pumps water uphill at low demand and releases it through turbines at peak times.
A dam across an estuary that generates electricity from the rise and fall of the tide.
The breakdown of organic waste without oxygen, which produces biogas.

factCards.definition: A high, exposed upland or coastal site with strong winds; away from houses (noise, shadow flicker); near an access road for construction; close to the grid (a transmission line); not in a protected area or on deep peat, ideally on land of low farming value.

questions.prompt: Examine the environmental impact of burning fossil fuels.
questions.model: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, smoke and fine particles. Carbon dioxide traps heat and enhances the greenhouse effect, causing global warming. Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides form acid rain, when they dissolve in water vapour to make sulphuric and nitric acids. Normal rain has a pH of about 5.6, and acid rain is below that. Acid rain is transboundary: emissions from Britain and Germany were carried by south-westerly winds to Norway and Sweden. The Black Triangle, where lignite-burning power stations killed forests in the 1970s and 1980s, shows the scale of the problem. Acid rain damaged German forests in the 1980s, and thousands of Scandinavian lakes were acidified and lost their fish. It also dissolves limestone and marble buildings and statues. Responses include the 1979 Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution, EU directives on large power stations, flue-gas desulphurisation at power stations such as Moneypoint, low-sulphur fuels, catalytic converters on cars from 1993, and liming of lakes in Sweden and Norway. As a result, European SO2 emissions have fallen by well over three-quarters since 1990. Smog is another impact. Burning coal and turf in homes produces smoke, and in cold, calm winter weather a temperature inversion traps it near the ground. Smog causes bronchitis, asthma and heart and lung disease. London's Great Smog of 1952 killed about 4,000 people at the time and led to the Clean Air Act 1956. In Dublin, severe winter smogs in the early 1980s led to a ban on the sale of smoky coal from 1 September 1990, which cut black smoke by about 70% and was linked by a 2002 Lancet study to about 350 fewer deaths a year. The ban was extended to Cork in 1995. Other impacts include oil spills, landscape damage from coal mining and peat cutting, and thermal pollution from power-station cooling water.

questions.prompt: With reference to one specific renewable energy source, explain its economic and environmental advantages.
questions.model: This answer uses wind energy. Economically, wind reduces Ireland's fossil-fuel import bill, which was about three-quarters of its energy in the early 2020s, and improves energy security. Wind supplied about a third of Irish electricity in the early 2020s, and Ireland's strong, frequent Atlantic winds give it a good resource. Wind farms create jobs and income in rural areas, and Irish sites such as Galway Wind Park, Connemara, and the offshore Arklow Bank Wind Park show the growth of the industry. Environmentally, wind produces no CO2, SO2 or NOx once a farm is built, so it helps Ireland meet its Climate Action Plan target of 80% renewable electricity by 2030 and avoid penalties for missing EU targets. Wind is also a free fuel once the turbines are built. The balancing disadvantage is that output varies with the wind, and local objections arise over noise, shadow flicker and visual impact.

questions.prompt: Explain why nuclear energy is not used to generate electricity in Ireland.
questions.model: The Electricity Regulation Act 1999 bans the use of nuclear fission to generate electricity in Ireland. The ESB planned a nuclear station at Carnsore Point, Co. Wexford, in the 1970s, but large public protests led to its abandonment. Fears raised by the Chernobyl accident in 1986 and by the Sellafield discharges into the Irish Sea added to the opposition. Other reasons include the risk of radioactive waste, the very high cost of building a plant, and the small size of Ireland's electricity grid.
